To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the fractionation of heavy metals (Cu, Zn, As and Cd) and the recovery of arsenic in the BCR scheme is highly dependent on the sample type, i.e. SRMs versus heavily contaminated samples, and that the fractionation schemes proposed in this thesis can be applied for arsenic in the SRMs, while the fractionation and recovery of arsenic are not reliable in the heavily contaminated soil samples.

(1) The BCR-scheme can be applied for fractionation of arsenic in SRMs, but not in heavily contaminated samples; (2) The Manful scheme is applicable for fractionation of both arsenic in SRM and heavily contaminated samples; and (3) The BCR and the Manful schemes can be applied for sequential extraction of other heavy metals (Mn, Fe, Zn, Pb, Cd) in both SRM and heavily-contaminated samples.

(1) The BCR sequential extraction scheme can not be used for arsenic speciation in SRMs, because of low recovery rates, (2) the phosphorus-like scheme can be used for arsenicspeciation in SRMs and in heavily contaminated samples, but (3) the scheme has to be modified for better recovery and (4) it has to be applied in the same manner to both SRMs and heavily contaminated samples.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a reliable and reproducible sequential extraction method for the speciation of arsenics and other heavy metals in solid environmental matrices.
the development and application of sequential extraction schemes for the fractionation of arsenic, manganese, copper, zinc, cadmium and lead in soils.

the application of sequential extraction schemes to the determination of solid phase speciation, and with the development of sequential extraction schemes for the determination of arsenic speciation in soil samples.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the BCR scheme for metal fractionation is applicable to the SRM samples, but the scheme has to be adapted and modified for the heavy metal and arsenic contaminated soil samples.
the BCR scheme is the most suitable for metal fractionation and the phosphorus-like scheme is the most promising scheme for arsenic speciation.
the BCR-schemes are applicable for fractionation of metals in SRM samples but the extraction schemes for arsenic should be modified.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the BCR-schemes are applicable to a wide variety of soil samples.
the sequential extractions applied to the SRM 2711 (Glasgow soil) and 2710 (montana soil) are not suitable for arsenic speciation.
the BCR-schemes for heavy metals are suitable for the fractionation of arsenic, but the recovery rate for this element is lower compared to heavy metals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the fractionation and recovery of arsenic in the BCR sequential extractions are not satisfactory.
the BCR sequential scheme is a useful tool for the determination of the speciation of heavy metal elements in soils.
the sequential extraction schemes can be used as a tool to assess the availability of contaminants and their mobility in soils and sediments.
